cards.text: Whoever wrote this psalm doesn't sign his name, friend, and he doesn't need a name tag. He opens LOUD by telling everybody to give thanks to the LORD. Then he gives the reason.

cards.question: The psalm opens by telling everyone to give thanks to the LORD. What's the first reason it gives?
The psalm says the LORD's loving devotion lasts only as long as His people deserve it.

cards.text: Then he calls on one crowd to speak up first: the redeemed of the LORD. If God ever pulled you out of something, this is your cue, and friend, I spent YEARS in a junk drawer, so my hand is UP.

cards.question: The redeemed of the LORD are called to speak up. What did He redeem them from?
The LORD didn't just rescue His redeemed. He gathered them from the lands. From where?

cards.text: East, west, north AND south? That's not a reunion, friend, that's EVERYBODY. Then the psalm paints its first picture: people wandering in desert wastelands.

cards.question: Out in the desert wastelands, the wanderers can't find a path to a city where they could live.

cards.text: Ever had the GPS say recalculating five times in a row, friend? These folks are hungry, thirsty and fainting inside, and they don't even HAVE a GPS to yell at.

cards.question: Lost, hungry and fainting in the desert, the wanderers cry out to ___ in their trouble.

cards.text: They cry out, and He delivers them from their distress. And He doesn't just send directions, friend. He leads them.

cards.question: The wanderers couldn't find any path. So the LORD led them on a ___ path to reach a city where they could live.
The wanderers finally have a city to live in. What does the psalm call on them to do now?
The reason the wanderers should give thanks: the LORD satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things.

cards.text: Second picture, and it's darker. Literally: these people sit in darkness and the shadow of death, prisoners in affliction and chains.

cards.question: The psalm says these prisoners ended up in darkness and chains even though they never went against God.

cards.text: So He humbles their hearts with hard labor, and they stumble with no one to help. Like dropping everything in a parking lot while every single person just keeps on walking.

cards.question: The prisoners cry out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saves them and brings them out of the darkness. What does He do with their chains?
That thanks line from the wanderers comes back for the prisoners. This time the reason is something the LORD has broken down. What is it?

cards.text: Third picture, and the psalm doesn't sugarcoat it. It calls these folks fools, suffering affliction because of their rebellious ways and their iniquities.

cards.question: The fools get so sick that they can't stand the thought of any food.
The fools are so sick that they draw near to what?

cards.text: And here it comes again: they cry out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saves them from their distress. I'm seeing a pattern here, friend, and I LOVE this pattern.

cards.question: The fools are near death, and they cry out. How does the LORD heal them?
The thanks line comes back a third time. Then the psalm says the healed should keep their thanks quiet and private.

cards.text: Fourth picture, and we're heading out to sea. Others go out in ships, doing business on the mighty waters.

cards.question: What do these traders see out on the deep?
One of the LORD's wonders out on the deep is anything but calm. What does He speak into being?

cards.text: It's up to the heavens, then down to the depths, and their courage melts in their anguish. That's every roller coaster I ever swore I'd never ride again, and NOBODY is letting these guys off.

cards.question: Tossed up and down by the storm, the sailors reel and stagger like ___.
These traders know the sea, so their skill gets them through the storm.

cards.text: So they cry out to the LORD in their trouble, and He brings them out of their distress. You know that one number in your phone you call when everything goes sideways? These folks KNOW who to call.

cards.question: The storm is raging. What does the LORD do to it?
The waves are hushed, and the sailors ___ in the silence.

cards.text: Then He guides them to the harbor they desired. After a storm like that, friend, I would kiss that dock with this WHOLE mustache.

cards.question: The thanks line comes back a fourth time. Then the psalm tells the sailors where to praise the LORD. Where?

cards.text: Now the pictures stop and the psalm zooms out to show what the LORD can do. He turns rivers into deserts, and springs of water into thirsty ground.

cards.question: The LORD even turns fruitful land into fields of salt. Why?
The same LORD who turns rivers into deserts can also turn a desert into pools of water.

cards.text: Remember the wanderers who couldn't find a city to live in? Here the LORD settles the hungry right where the desert used to be, and they build a city, sow fields, plant vineyards and bring in a fruitful harvest.

cards.question: The LORD blesses these settlers, but He lets their herds dwindle away.

cards.text: But life still has hard seasons. Sometimes they're decreased and humbled by oppression, evil and sorrow.

cards.question: Then the psalm turns to the nobles. The LORD pours out contempt on them. What else does He do to them?
But the LORD lifts the ___ from affliction and increases their families like flocks.

cards.text: The nobles knocked down, the needy lifted up. And the upright are watching all of it.

cards.question: The upright see the LORD lift up the needy, and they ___.

cards.text: And all iniquity shuts its mouth. Just goes QUIET, like the oven timer when I finally find the right button.

cards.question: The psalm's last line says let the wise pay heed to these things. And what should they consider?

findings.problem: The question says the LORD gathered them 'from the lands' (plural). That rules out the two single-place wrong answers, 'From Egypt alone' and 'From Babylon alone'. The matching 'alone' wording on both wrong answers also makes the right answer stand out.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The GPS comparison is blended into the Bible setting ('they don't even HAVE a GPS to yell at'). The joke's action, being lost, also doesn't match the fact this card tells, which is hunger, thirst and fainting.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: 'So He humbles their hearts with hard labor' adds a cause-and-effect link that verse 12 doesn't state. The text never says the humbling happened because of the rebellion in verse 11.

rule.text: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: Verse 13 (they cry out and He saves them) is only told inside this choice card's question. No story card sets it up.

rule.text: The setup for a choice is on a story card.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop: 6 multiple choice, 4 true or false and only 2 fill in the blank.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop: 6 multiple choice, 3 true or false and only 2 fill in the blank. This is also close to the pattern in stop 1.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'The wonders of the LORD', is a broad, Bible-sounding category. The wrong answers are specific objects ('A great fish', 'A pillar of fire'). They aren't the same kind of thing, so the right answer stands out. A baker could also argue that a great fish counts among His wonders in the deep.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin says he swore off roller coasters he rode. That adds a new experience to his backstory outside his bakery. The line 'NOBODY is letting these guys off' also blends the roller coaster image with the sailors.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: Asking what the sailors stagger like ('drunkards' vs 'wounded men' vs 'blind men') is guessing the poem's exact simile. A baker can't reason it out from context.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card packs in more than two beats: the callback to the wanderers, the LORD settling the hungry and building a city, and sowing fields, planting vineyards and harvesting.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The question says the LORD pours out contempt on the nobles. That rules out the two positive wrong answers ('Seats them beside kings', 'Gives them more land').

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Verse 42 says only 'The upright see and rejoice', without saying what they see. The question fills it in as seeing the LORD lift up the needy.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.
